extracted.intended_audience: writers (humorists, copywriters, content marketers) and editors seeking practical writing rules
extracted.subtask_description: A short set of ten practical, editor-tested rules for writing funny, engaging, and persuasive content (originally from The Onion’s founding editor). Applicable to satire, long- and short-form content, headlines, and marketing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept is king.
rubrics_metrics.description: "What’s going to make your content stand out?" — your concept (headline/title) is the flag you’re raising; if it’s not the right concept you’re sunk before you write a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the joke/concept first so people are engaged immediately. In an attention economy the headline must address a personal problem or promise to answer a burning question. Equate concept with headline/title: it must grab attention. To choose the right concept, start with your target audience: what pleasures are they seeking? what pains are they trying to assuage?

rubrics_metrics.name: The key to quality is quantity.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Basically, 95% of everything we create is garbage." — professional practice relies on generating lots of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate a high volume of ideas (example: each writer bringing ~20 headlines to a weekly meeting). Quality improves with quantity: from abundance you can select a dozen strong pieces. Expect most ideas to be poor; use deliberate overproduction to surface the best material (late-night monologues and The Onion both use selection-from-many).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words.
rubrics_metrics.description: "The shorter the better." — remove superfluous words; cutting even a single syllable can make a joke punchier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trimming reduces dilution, speeds the reader, and sharpens the message. When editing, always look to reduce; if cutting reveals you have nothing to say, that’s valuable feedback. This principle applies across genres: concise prose often communicates the core more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruffle some feathers.
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is how your message will stand the test of time." — effective satire often offends; Horatian (gentle) satire is forgettable, Juvenalian (biting) satire challenges power and lasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your goal is gentle amusement or biting critique. Satire that angers or offends (addresses perceived social evils, speaks truth to power) is more likely to be remembered. Know your content’s message and whether you intend to provoke; pushing buttons can give cultural longevity to your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t fall in love.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Kill your darlings." — don’t become so attached to an idea that you ignore feedback or refuse to move on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attachment to a single idea is especially common for new writers with few pieces to their name. If you’re unwilling to hear critique or pivot, that attachment becomes a barrier to serving the audience. Prioritize reader response and usefulness over personal attachment to wording or concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Detail almost always makes writing better." — specificity (sensory detail, concrete imagery) improves clarity and emotional impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crisp details that appeal to the senses to paint a mental picture without verbosity (example: Salinger excerpt). Specifics help readers feel emotion and make the piece more engaging; they also make jokes and arguments more vivid and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread.
rubrics_metrics.description: "It’s a mode of conveying professionalism." — small mistakes undermine perceived competence and opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check grammar, spelling, and syntax before submitting. Even if the material is strong, careless errors can cost jobs or publication. Proofreading is a low-effort way to increase credibility and your chances of achieving goals (getting hired, being published, connecting with readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don’t tell.
rubrics_metrics.description: "You’re going to be so much more effective at engaging an audience if you do." — show character traits and situations through action/details rather than stating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples, analogies, and literary devices to create images and feelings rather than flat exposition. The article uses an extreme comedic example ("Bob just stabbed a baby through the heart!") to illustrate showing vs telling. Hide the overt message sometimes and let readers infer, which increases engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it accessible.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your writing needs to be understandable to just about every level of reader." — avoid density and unnecessary prerequisites for understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so people can access your work without specialized caveats or prior knowledge. In the attention economy, authorial intent and obscure references are liabilities; the onus is on the writer to make their point clear. Ask yourself: How can I make this more clear?

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your joke and make sure the reader knows your joke.
rubrics_metrics.description: "Always be in control." — be explicit about your point and structure the piece so readers understand the joke/subtext and laugh at the intended target/time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize like a speech (tell them what you’ll say, say it, tell them what you said). Understand your joke’s subtext, the 'funny filters' you’re using, and how arrangement leads the audience to the intended reaction. Control the reader’s experience by clarifying topic, audience, and purpose so the effect lands as intended.
